rules.name: 3rd-Person Singular -s
rules.explain: Singular subjects (he/she/it, and singular names) take the -s verb form in the present simple. Plural subjects, and 'I'/'you', take the base form.

singular.note: Singular subject → add -s to the verb.

plural.text: Albus and Severus go to the market.
plural.note: Plural subject → use the base form, no -s.

rules.name: Collective Nouns as a Unit
rules.explain: Collective nouns (team, committee, family) take a singular verb when acting as one group. Words for the individual members (players, people) take a plural verb.

singular.note: Collective noun acting as one unit → singular verb.

plural.note: Naming the individual members → plural verb.

rules.name: Indefinite Pronouns
rules.explain: Pronouns ending in -one, -body, or -thing (everyone, nobody, something) are always singular. Few, many, several, and both are always plural.

plural.note: Few, many, several, and both are always plural.

rules.name: Either/Or, Neither/Nor — Proximity Rule
rules.explain: With either...or and neither...nor, the verb agrees with whichever subject is closest to it — not with the first one.

singular.text: Either the employees or the manager is responsible.
singular.note: Verb agrees with the closer subject — here, singular 'manager'.

plural.text: Either the manager or the employees are responsible.
plural.note: Verb agrees with the closer subject — here, plural 'employees'.

items.before: Either the manager or the employees
Either the employees or the manager
Neither the teacher nor the students
Neither the students nor the teacher

rules.name: 'A Number Of' vs 'The Number Of'
rules.explain: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb. 'The number of' refers to the total count itself, which is a single figure — singular.

singular.note: 'The number of' refers to one total figure → singular.
